04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The archivist's response did not open the private correspondence file. Instead, it exposed a weakness in the story Emma had almost begun to tell herself. The entry catalogued as “Student Travel — decision not received” was dated 12 October 2011, but its heading had been supplied by newspaper staff. It might summarise the letter accurately; it could not safely be treated as the writer's own testimony.

Emma entered the date and provenance separately. The item postdated Claire's disappearance, although that sequence furnished no causal link. A temporal coincidence could make a lead worth examining without making it evidence of a connection.

Sarah called as soon as Emma forwarded the archivist's explanation.

“Somebody must have complained about not receiving a decision.”

“Possibly. What we actually possess is a description in an index. We don't know whether the writer was an applicant, whether the decision was delayed or whether the phrase even reflects the complaint's exact wording.”

At the trust, Fiona Bell's records team had made another modest discovery. No verified log of returned decision notices had been identified, but a blank form headed “Contact attempt” survived. Its fields provided for an application reference, a date and the action taken. Fiona had found no completed example and cautioned against assuming that every return, or indeed any particular return, had been followed up.

Placed beside the office manual, the form supplied a plausible mechanism for documenting renewed contact after undelivered post. It did not demonstrate the mechanism's operation. Emma was struck by how many pieces of paperwork described desirable administrative behaviour while leaving the underlying events inaccessible.

Sarah proposed locating the author of the October letter. Emma preferred a less intrusive question. She asked whether the archivist could count the surviving subject-index entries connected with the student travel scheme while keeping names and original correspondence confidential. Even a count would require qualification: a partial index could neither exclude additional letters nor establish that its entries represented different people.

The archivist undertook to check what could be established. Fiona likewise offered to continue searching for records explaining how uncertain delivery had been handled. Neither promised a conclusive result.

Emma reopened the review guidance. It made receipt of a decision the starting point for a fourteen-day period in which an unsuccessful applicant could seek reconsideration. A record of dispatch fell short of that event; an unused contact form fell shorter still. If the trust had applied the deadline from the posting date, fairness questions might arise. But Emma had no evidence that it had done so, nor that any applicant had been prevented from appealing.

She wrote two headings on a clean page: Potential procedural vulnerability and Documented individual failure. The first column contained a question about proof of receipt. The second remained empty. That absence was not a verdict in the trust's favour or against it; it was a boundary around what she could responsibly publish.

Her next request would therefore concern the rule itself, not an imagined victim: what evidence, if any, had the trust required before treating a decision as received and starting the review clock?

At last she had a question that could be answered without first deciding who was guilty.
